items.title: Gdynia Outer Port PPP: bid deadline 30 September, two shortlisted bidders have Chinese links
items.original_title: Gdynia Outer Port PPP: bid deadline 30 September, two shortlisted bidders have Chinese links
items.summary:
The Port of Gdynia Authority extended to 30 September 2026 the deadline for four shortlisted consortia to bid for the Outer Port container terminal, to be developed as a public-private partnership. It is Poland's largest PPP procedure by estimated value, with the selected partner expected to finance roughly USD 1.31bn and jointly operate the terminal.

Two of the four bidders have Chinese connections: Mota-Engil Central Europe, whose parent is 32.4% owned by state-owned China Communications Construction Company, and a Hutchison Ports Poland–Port of Felixstowe consortium. Hutchison has wholly owned Gdynia Container Terminal since 2004.

The Outer Port is planned as dual-use infrastructure supporting NATO military mobility. Gdynia hosts NATO exercises, is a major arrival point for US military cargo, and neighbours Gdynia Naval Base; the adjacent Baltic Container Terminal already serves as a military transhipment hub.
items.why: Decides who operates new container capacity in Gdynia and how security screening shapes foreign investment in Polish ports; watch for the award decision now that bids are due.

items.title: Port of Gdańsk posts record 41.7 Mt in H1 2026; coal up 51%, grain up 13%
items.original_title: Port of Gdańsk posts record 41.7 Mt in H1 2026; coal up 51%, grain up 13%
items.summary:
The Port of Gdańsk handled a record 41.7 million tonnes in the first half of 2026, up 9% year on year. Liquid fuels made up 45% of volumes at 18.8 Mt (98% of the H1 2025 level). General cargo reached 15.2 Mt (+17%), including 13.8 Mt of containers and 1.6 million TEU at Baltic Hub.

Among bulk cargoes, coal rose 51% to 4.3 Mt, which the port attributes to winter conditions; grain rose 13% to almost 1.3 Mt; other bulk was 1.8 Mt (95% of last year); ore rose 7% to 173,000 t; timber jumped 178% to 81,000 t. Imports were 27.8 Mt, exports 8.3 Mt and transit 5.6 Mt, across 2,193 vessel calls.
items.why: Benchmark for competitor volumes in coal, grain and other dry bulk, the core cargoes of Szczecin–Świnoujście and Gdynia.

items.title: Construction of Cape Pomerania container port in Świnoujście formally launched
items.original_title: Construction of Cape Pomerania container port in Świnoujście formally launched
items.summary:
Poland has formally launched the Cape Pomerania deepwater port and container terminal in Świnoujście, a PLN 10bn (about EUR 2.3bn) project and the largest investment in the 75-year history of the Szczecin and Świnoujście Seaports Authority.

The design includes a 17-metre-deep basin and a 1.3-km main quay able to berth up to three ocean-going container ships at once, including two up to 400 metres long. The infrastructure minister put expected capacity at around 2 million TEU a year.

The project is meant to establish Poland as a major container hub for Central and Eastern Europe. Originally planned under the previous government, the facility will serve both civilian and defence purposes.
items.why: Will reshape traffic, hinterland rail demand and land use around Świnoujście, where the group operates; who operates the terminal is still to be decided.

items.title: New EU steel safeguard: 18.3 Mt duty-free quota, 50% tariff above it, melt-and-pour disclosure
items.original_title: New EU steel safeguard: 18.3 Mt duty-free quota, 50% tariff above it, melt-and-pour disclosure
items.summary:
A new EU steel safeguard regulation took effect on 1 July 2026, replacing the previous safeguard. It sets an annual duty-free import quota of 18.3 million tonnes across 26 steel product categories, with a 50% tariff on volumes above the quota.

Half of the quota is reserved for free-trade-agreement partners, which supply about 80% of EU steel imports; the other half is open to all partners. Importers must now disclose where the steel was melted and poured. The Commission negotiated the quotas under WTO Article XXVIII, and many partners have tentatively accepted their allocations.
items.why: Steel products are a priority growth cargo for the group; tighter quotas and the 50% duty change import volumes and their routing through Baltic ports.
